paragraphs: This paper examines why relatively simple transformers can outperform more elaborate designs on common time-series forecasting benchmarks. It focuses on how models turn measurements into tokens: individual time points, stretches of time, or separate variables. These choices determine which relationships attention can directly examine and help frame questions about where forecasting gains actually come from.

Using mutual-information analysis and synthetic datasets, the researchers find that relationships within a variable contribute most to benchmark prediction performance. Relationships between different variables contribute comparatively little. They also identify normalization using Z-scores and skip connections as crucial components, showing that attention design alone does not explain the success of simpler models.

The interpretation depends heavily on the data. The benchmark series largely depend on their own histories and have stationary behavior, conditions that favor learning within-variable patterns. The paper also validates its findings on real healthcare data. Its practical contribution is to connect architectural choices to dataset properties, rather than treating benchmark success as evidence that one attention strategy will work equally well everywhere.
icml-2025-a-closer-look-at-transformers-.tldr: Simple forecasting transformers succeed largely through within-variable dependencies and key architectural components, with results strongly shaped by benchmark properties.

paragraphs: AffinityFlow addresses antibody affinity maturation: choosing mutations that improve how strongly an antibody binds its target. The study considers a setting where the available inputs are only the antibody and antigen sequences. Although the inputs are sequences, the method uses generated protein structures internally to help search for promising changes.

The approach alternates between structure and sequence optimization. First, it holds the sequence fixed and guides structure generation toward stronger predicted binding, building on AlphaFlow's sequence-conditioned structure generation. Next, inverse folding proposes sequence mutations from structures, and a sequence-based predictor refines those proposals. This creates a cycle in which structural and sequence information both influence the search.

Training the two predictors is difficult because labeled affinity data are scarce. AffinityFlow addresses this with co-teaching: each predictor selects consensus samples to help refine the other, drawing useful information from noisy biophysical energies. The authors report state-of-the-art results in proof-of-concept maturation experiments. These findings support the alternating approach in the tested setting, while retaining the study's explicit proof-of-concept scope.
icml-2025-affinityflow-guided-flows-for-.tldr: AffinityFlow alternates guided structure generation and sequence mutation, using mutually trained predictors to improve antibody affinity in proof-of-concept experiments.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to select a size-limited set when the objective has diminishing returns but adding an item can sometimes reduce its value. The computational challenge is to find a valuable set while allowing many objective evaluations to happen in parallel. The authors focus on combinatorial algorithms that work with discrete selections.

Their main randomized algorithm achieves an approximation ratio of 1/e minus epsilon, reaching arbitrarily close to the established 1/e benchmark for continuous methods. They also develop a simpler algorithm with a weaker ratio of 1/4 minus epsilon, guaranteed with probability at least 1 minus 1/n. This provides two choices with different guarantees and practical behavior.

Both algorithms require O(log(n) log(k)) sequential rounds of adaptive computation and O(n log(n) log(k)) objective queries. Thus, the approximation result does not imply matching the continuous approach's O(log(n)) adaptivity. Experiments show competitive objective values, with the simpler algorithm particularly economical in queries. The contribution is a strong approximation guarantee using a parallel combinatorial approach, alongside a simpler practical alternative.
icml-2025-breaking-barriers-combinatoria.tldr: Two parallel combinatorial algorithms offer strong approximation guarantees for size-constrained non-monotone submodular maximization, including a ratio approaching 1/e.

paragraphs: CodeSteer addresses a coordination problem in language-model reasoning: deciding when to reason in text and when to generate code for symbolic computation. Its central idea is to train a separate guiding model that steers a larger model through these choices over multiple turns. Symbolic and self-answer checkers supplement the guidance.

The researchers construct SymBench, containing 37 symbolic tasks with adjustable difficulty, and synthesize 12,000 guidance-and-generation trajectories plus 5,500 guidance comparison pairs. They train Llama-3-8B using multi-turn supervised fine-tuning and direct preference optimization. The resulting CodeSteerLLM learns to guide another model's problem-solving process rather than simply serving as the final answer generator.

On SymBench, adding CodeSteer to GPT-4o raises its average score from 53.3 to 86.4, exceeding the reported scores of the named comparison models across the benchmark. The tasks include 28 seen and nine unseen tasks. Guidance trained for GPT-4o also transfers to Claude, Mistral, and GPT-3.5, with a reported average boost of 41.8. These results support learned coordination of text and code as a way to improve symbolic problem solving.
icml-2025-codesteer-symbolic-augmented-l.tldr: CodeSteer trains a smaller guiding model to coordinate larger models' text reasoning and code generation, substantially improving tested symbolic-task performance.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether randomizing value estimates can help multiple reinforcement-learning agents explore an environment concurrently. Such methods already had support in single-agent settings, but their benefit for concurrent exploration needed theoretical justification. The authors adapt randomized least-squares value iteration to a framework that also uses aggregated representations of states.

They establish polynomial worst-case regret bounds for both finite- and infinite-horizon environments. Regret measures the shortfall in reward relative to the benchmark used in the analysis. In both settings, per-agent regret decreases at the optimal rate proportional to one over the square root of the number of agents. The result gives a precise theoretical account of the benefit of concurrent learning.

The algorithm also trades memory against the regret bound: relative to the cited earlier methods, it reduces space requirements by a factor of K while increasing worst-case regret by only a square-root-of-K factor. The authors additionally obtain a square-root-of-H improvement over one earlier bound through a different algorithmic and proof approach. Numerical experiments accompany the theory, linking the formal analysis to observed behavior.
icml-2025-concurrent-reinforcement-learn.tldr: Randomized value iteration with aggregated states gives concurrent agents provable exploration benefits and a quantified tradeoff between memory and regret.

paragraphs: High-resolution terrain data make it possible to represent landscapes in great detail, but they also create very large graphs for distance calculations. This paper tackles shortest-path-distance queries on digital elevation models. Its goal is to answer these queries approximately and quickly using a compact learned data structure.

The method builds on neural geodesic fields, which use a neural representation to estimate distances. The authors introduce a decoupled version of NeuroGF together with a two-stage mixed-training procedure. These changes reduce computational bottlenecks during learning, allowing the method to train on terrain models at scales that the earlier approach could not feasibly handle.

Experiments cover synthetic and real terrain datasets. One reported example trains a model with roughly 70,000 parameters on a terrain containing 16 million nodes within hours. It answers distance queries with 1% relative error in at most 10 milliseconds per query. This example illustrates the central benefit: a small learned representation can provide fast approximate distance answers even when the underlying terrain graph is very large.
icml-2025-de-coupled-neurogf-for-shortes.tldr: A decoupled neural distance representation and two-stage training make fast approximate shortest-path queries feasible on terrain graphs with millions of nodes.

paragraphs: Pruning reduces a language model's parameter count by removing selected weights. Applying the same pruning rate to every layer can damage performance when sparsity is high, because layers contribute differently to the model's behavior. Earlier non-uniform approaches address this imbalance but often depend on values fixed in advance.

Dynamic Layerwise Pruning estimates relative layer importance using both model weights and input activations. It then assigns pruning rates based on those estimates. The key change is to let information about the model and its response to inputs determine how pruning is distributed, rather than committing to a uniform or predefined allocation.

Experiments across multiple language models show that DLP preserves performance effectively at high sparsity. At 70% sparsity on LLaMA2-7B, the authors report a perplexity reduction of 7.79 and an average accuracy improvement of 2.7% over state-of-the-art methods. They also report compatibility with existing compression techniques and parameter-efficient fine-tuning. These findings make layerwise allocation an important part of the compression strategy, alongside the choice of which individual weights to remove.
icml-2025-dlp-dynamic-layerwise-pruning-.tldr: DLP uses weights and input activations to assign layer-specific pruning rates, improving performance retention at high sparsity.

paragraphs: Core-set selection aims to identify a small, informative subset of training examples so that deep learning can use data more efficiently. Selecting that subset is itself a challenge: existing approaches often depend on heuristics or complicated optimization. This paper introduces a selection objective intended to connect efficiency with the training progress made by individual examples.

The objective minimizes the sum of squared losses over all samples while adaptively balancing losses between selected and unselected examples. From this objective, the authors derive Maximum Reduction as Maximum Contribution, or MRMC. This criterion treats the examples associated with the greatest loss reduction as those contributing most to overall convergence.

The method also adds a balance constraint so that contributions from the chosen core-set are distributed evenly. Selection therefore considers both how much an example helps and how contributions are spread across the subset. Experiments report substantial improvements in training efficiency while preserving model performance at minimal cost. The central contribution is an explicit optimization-based rationale for choosing informative data, together with a balancing mechanism that shapes the resulting core-set.
icml-2025-efficient-core-set-selection-f.tldr: MRMC selects training subsets through a squared-loss objective that rewards loss reduction and balances contributions, improving efficiency while preserving performance.

paragraphs: Counterfactual reasoning asks how an outcome would differ under an alternative course of events. This paper studies complete counterfactual identifiability: whether every structural causal model satisfying the stated assumptions gives consistent answers to all causal questions. The concern is agreement among admissible models, so that counterfactual conclusions do not depend on an unresolved choice of model.

The authors introduce exogenous isomorphism and an associated notion of identifiability to simplify this problem. They investigate sufficient assumptions in two special model classes. For bijective structural causal models, their analysis uses counterfactual transport. For triangular monotonic structural causal models, it extends work on identifiability at the intervention level of the Pearl Causal Hierarchy.

These results unify and generalize existing theoretical accounts, providing guarantees under the investigated assumptions. The paper also develops neural triangular monotonic models to address consistency in counterfactual reasoning and reports experiments supporting the method and theory. The important distinction is that the assumptions are sufficient conditions within specified model classes; the findings do not establish unrestricted counterfactual identification for arbitrary causal models.
icml-2025-exogenous-isomorphism-for-coun.tldr: Exogenous isomorphism provides a framework for sufficient conditions that make counterfactual answers consistent across specified classes of causal models.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether a simple process operating on compressed representations can capture useful structure in natural images. The process, called FINOLA, combines normalization with linear autoregressive updates. Experiments show that it can reconstruct images with high fidelity without being supplied explicit positional information, motivating a closer look at what its learned dynamics represent.

The analysis focuses on two learned coefficient matrices. Across training runs, the authors observe that these matrices are typically invertible and that the product of one with the other's inverse is diagonalizable. This observed structure permits an interpretation of the latent dynamics as a system resembling one-way wave equations.

Within that interpretation, each image corresponds to a unique solution of the equations in compressed latent space. The result suggests that simple shared dynamic laws may help describe image structure and invariance. This is an empirical observation and a mathematical interpretation of the learned process, rather than a claim that all natural images must obey universal wave laws. It opens a route for modeling images through the evolution of their latent representations.
icml-2025-exploring-invariance-in-images.tldr: FINOLA reconstructs images from compressed representations, and observed matrix structure lets its latent dynamics be interpreted as one-way wave equations.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks have shown promise for guiding quadratic-program solvers and directly predicting approximate solutions. This paper asks a more fundamental question: which properties of these optimization problems can such networks represent at all? It studies quadratic programs with linear constraints, separating problems with continuous variables from those that also impose integer requirements.

In the continuous setting, the authors prove that message-passing graph neural networks can universally represent several central properties. These include feasibility, the optimal objective value, and optimal solutions. The result provides a theoretical basis for using these networks to capture information that is directly relevant to solving a quadratic program.

The mixed-integer setting has a different answer. Here, graph neural networks are not universal approximators, although the authors identify a subclass of problems that they can reliably represent. This distinction matters when interpreting successful applications: expressive capacity depends on the problem class. The paper's contribution concerns what the networks can represent in theory, rather than an empirical claim that every representable problem can be learned or solved quickly.
icml-2025-expressive-power-of-graph-neur.tldr: Message-passing GNNs can universally represent key properties of continuous linearly constrained quadratic programs, but have expressiveness limits in the mixed-integer setting.

paragraphs: Generative zero-shot learning creates training features for classes without observed training examples. Existing methods often generate those features from expert-annotated semantic descriptions. GenZSL instead draws on similar seen classes and uses semantic vectors obtained from target class names through CLIP text embeddings, reducing reliance on detailed expert-provided class descriptions.

The method uses an inductive variational autoencoder to generate new class samples from this combination of familiar classes and target-name information. It adds two mechanisms to make those samples more useful for classifier training. Class diversity promotion increases diversity among semantic vectors, while a target-class-guided information objective directs optimization toward information relevant to the intended class.

Experiments on three benchmark datasets report improvements in both effectiveness and efficiency. On AWA2, the authors report a 24.7% performance gain and training more than 60 times faster than f-VAEGAN. These results support transferring information from similar seen classes as a productive basis for generating unseen-class features. The reported comparison also shows that replacing richer expert descriptions with class-name embeddings can work well within the tested approach.
icml-2025-genzsl-generative-zero-shot-le.tldr: GenZSL generates unseen-class features from similar seen classes and class-name embeddings, improving benchmark performance and training efficiency.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning often assumes that augmented versions of an example retain a consistent label. Strong or random transformations, such as random resized cropping, can violate that assumption. This paper calls the probability of such a violation labeling error and studies how it affects later classification using the learned representation.

The authors establish several negative effects on downstream classification risk. They then apply dimensionality reduction, including singular value decomposition, to the original data to reduce false positive samples. Both theoretical analysis and experiments examine this mitigation. However, reducing dimensionality can also weaken connectivity in the augmentation graph, producing a competing effect that may reduce classification accuracy.

The resulting recommendation is to balance small labeling error with strong graph connectivity. The authors suggest combining SVD, weak augmentation, data inflation, and a moderate embedding dimension. Dimensions of 512 and 1024 are examples from their experiments, rather than universal settings. The main insight is that preventing inconsistent augmented pairs is only part of the problem: preserving useful relationships among augmented samples also matters.
icml-2025-how-does-labeling-error-impact.tldr: Dimensionality reduction can reduce contrastive-learning labeling errors, but its benefits must be balanced against lost augmentation-graph connectivity.

paragraphs: KinDEL is a public dataset intended to support machine learning for drug discovery using DNA-encoded libraries. These libraries enable exploration of very large chemical spaces, but limited public data have restricted the development of learning methods. The dataset focuses on compounds studied against two kinases, MAPK14 and DDR1.

KinDEL includes 81 million compounds and combines two-dimensional chemical information with three-dimensional binding poses from molecular docking. The authors describe it as one of the largest public DNA-encoded-library datasets and the first to include such poses. Those poses are computational docking outputs, giving researchers structural information alongside the chemical representations used in the benchmark.

The resource also provides biophysical validation measurements both with and without DNA attached. The authors use these measurements to evaluate several machine-learning approaches, including new structure-based probabilistic models. This makes KinDEL both a large data resource and a benchmark connected to experimental validation. Its intended value is to support better data-driven identification of promising compounds, with a shared setting for evaluating methods that use chemical and structural information.
icml-2025-kindel-dna-encoded-library-dat.tldr: KinDEL provides 81 million compounds, docking poses, and biophysical validation data for benchmarking machine learning on two kinase targets.

paragraphs: Safety Polytope, or SaP, represents language-model safety through geometric constraints in the model's internal representation space. The method learns multiple boundaries that distinguish safe and unsafe regions. This gives the model an explicit geometric structure for detecting problematic behavior and steering representations toward compliance with the learned constraints.

SaP operates after model training and acts on representations without changing the model's weights. The same geometric framework supports both detection and correction: polytope facets identify unsafe regions, and geometric steering adjusts representations. The approach is designed to enforce safety constraints while preserving the capabilities already present in the underlying model.

Experiments across multiple language models show effective detection of unethical inputs and lower adversarial attack success rates while maintaining standard-task performance. Analysis also finds that different facets specialize in different semantic aspects of safety. This specialization offers a way to inspect how the learned constraints divide the safety problem. The evidence therefore supports both a practical intervention and a more interpretable representation of safety in the tested models.
icml-2025-learning-safety-constraints-fo.tldr: SaP learns geometric safety constraints in language-model representations, reducing successful attacks while preserving standard-task performance in experiments.

paragraphs: Sparse autoencoders decompose language-model representations into a small active set of linear latent vectors. Their reconstructions can be inserted into a model to study its behavior, but doing so often increases prediction loss. Improving the autoencoder using language-model gradients can also require many costly backward passes.

This paper takes a different optimization route: it keeps a previously trained sparse autoencoder and uses low-rank adaptation to fine-tune the language model around it. The study examines this approach across autoencoder sparsity and width, model size, adaptation rank, and layer placement. It also investigates adapting a model to multiple autoencoders simultaneously.

Across the tested Gemma Scope settings, the method reduces the cross-entropy loss gap caused by insertion by 30–55%. It reaches the same downstream loss as end-to-end autoencoders 3–20 times faster on Gemma-2-2B and 2–10 times faster on Llama-3.2-1B. Reported downstream metric improvements further support the approach. The broader finding is that optimizing the model itself can improve the tradeoffs involved in using sparse autoencoders for interpretability.
icml-2025-low-rank-adapting-models-for-s.tldr: Fine-tuning language models around existing sparse autoencoders reduces insertion-related prediction loss and reaches matched loss faster than end-to-end SAE training.

paragraphs: Latent diffusion models generate images through compressed representations produced by a tokenizer. This paper investigates which properties of those representations help diffusion learning and generation. Its theoretical and empirical analysis links better generation quality to more structured latent distributions, including fewer Gaussian mixture modes and features that distinguish semantic content more effectively.

Motivated by those findings, the authors introduce MAETok, an autoencoder trained with mask modeling. It aims to preserve reconstruction fidelity while creating a semantically rich latent space. The approach shows that an autoencoder can supply useful diffusion representations without requiring a variational formulation, focusing attention on the organization of the learned space.

Experiments report state-of-the-art ImageNet generation using 128 tokens. For images at 512 by 512 resolution, the paper reports a gFID of 1.69, training 76 times faster, and inference throughput 31 times higher in its comparisons. Together, these findings support latent-space structure as a crucial design consideration. They demonstrate that variational constraints are unnecessary for the reported success, rather than establishing that every ordinary autoencoder will produce equally effective diffusion representations.
icml-2025-masked-autoencoders-are-effect.tldr: MAETok uses masked autoencoding to create structured image latents that enable strong diffusion generation with only 128 tokens.

paragraphs: This paper develops search trees that use predicted item weights to decide how deeply items should sit in the tree. It builds on treaps, assigning each item a priority that combines a transformed predicted weight with uniform randomness. The design connects access predictions to tree organization through a simple priority rule.

When weights equal relative access frequencies, the resulting trees achieve static optimality. The analysis covers arbitrary input distributions, extending earlier learning-augmented search-tree results restricted to Zipfian distributions. The authors also generalize the approach to B-trees through a B-treap construction, carrying the central weighting idea into another search-tree structure.

The trees can reorganize online to exploit locality in access sequences and achieve the working-set property. They also support insertion, deletion, and prediction updates, and the authors establish robustness to prediction errors. An empirical study reports improvements over prior methods and classic structures. Together, these results address both the value of accurate predictions and the practical need for a tree to keep functioning as access patterns, stored items, and predictions change.
icml-2025-on-the-power-of-learning-augme.tldr: Prediction-weighted treap priorities yield robust, dynamic search trees with optimality guarantees extending to arbitrary access distributions.

paragraphs: Data collected for a machine-learning service can contain private attributes unrelated to the service's intended task. Protecting those attributes requires preserving useful information while limiting what the data reveal about private characteristics. This paper theoretically and empirically identifies a shared vulnerability in protection methods based on adversarial training.

PASS addresses that vulnerability by learning to replace an original sample with another sample according to a probability distribution. Protection therefore operates through stochastic substitution. The replacement probabilities are trained using a new loss derived from an information-theoretic objective that explicitly combines private-attribute protection with preservation of downstream utility.

The authors evaluate PASS on facial images, human-activity sensor signals, and voice recordings. Results across these different modalities support its effectiveness and generalizability. The variety of data matters because the proposed mechanism is intended to protect attributes without being tied to a single input format. The central contribution is an alternative to adversarial removal strategies, with a principled training objective for choosing substitutions that retain task-relevant information while protecting private attributes.
icml-2025-pass-private-attributes-protec.tldr: PASS learns probabilistic sample substitutions to protect private attributes while preserving downstream utility across several data modalities.

paragraphs: Long-context language models can process extensive documents, but generation is expensive. Conventional speculative decoding uses a smaller model to propose text, yet long-context key-value cache operations can make that drafting process memory-bound. RAPID changes the drafter's input by giving it a shortened context assembled through retrieval.

The resulting retrieval-augmented drafter proposes text for a target model operating on the longer context. Because the drafter handles less context, it can be the same size as the target model or even larger while remaining computationally efficient. RAPID also introduces inference-time knowledge transfer that enriches the target distribution using retrieval-augmented information, allowing stronger drafters to contribute to generation quality.

Experiments with LLaMA-3.1 and Qwen2.5 report quality improvements alongside more than twofold speedups for long-context inference. One example raises LLaMA-3.1-8B's InfiniteBench score from 39.33 to 42.83. Analyses also report robustness across tested context lengths and retrieval quality. The findings show how retrieval can support long-context generation by reducing drafting costs and supplying useful information during inference.
icml-2025-rapid-long-context-inference-w.tldr: RAPID uses short retrieved contexts for speculative drafting and inference-time knowledge transfer, improving long-context generation quality while more than doubling speed in experiments.

paragraphs: Private partition selection aims to release as many distinct items as possible from users' sets while maintaining user-level differential privacy. The item universe is unbounded. This problem appears in tasks such as extracting vocabulary from private text, reporting categorical statistics, and learning embeddings from user-provided items.

MaxAdaptiveDegree, or MAD, reallocates weight to improve which items can be released. Items with weight well above the privacy threshold give up some weight to items with less support, increasing the probability of releasing less frequent items. The method can run efficiently in massively parallel systems, and the authors prove stochastic dominance over the standard parallel algorithm.

The paper also introduces MAD2R, a two-round version that uses first-round results to guide second-round weighting toward releasing more items. Experiments report the best results among the parallel algorithms considered. The methods scale to datasets containing hundreds of billions of items, up to three orders of magnitude larger than those studied in prior work. The contribution combines a formal improvement over a standard approach with evidence of large-scale practicality.
icml-2025-scalable-private-partition-sel.tldr: MAD adaptively shifts excess item weight toward less frequent items, improving private partition selection while scaling to hundreds of billions of items.

paragraphs: When multimodal language models learn new tasks sequentially, their performance on earlier tasks can deteriorate for different reasons. This paper distinguishes superficial forgetting, where answers adopt an unsuitable format, from essential forgetting, where properly formatted answers become factually incorrect. Format failures can conceal whether the model still retains the relevant knowledge.

SEFE first addresses the format problem through Answer Style Diversification. This procedure transforms training data so that different tasks share similarly diversified answer styles, reducing the shifts in style that can make earlier responses unusable. Handling this issue also makes it easier to assess genuine loss of prior knowledge.

The second component, RegLoRA, targets essential forgetting. It regularizes LoRA weight-update matrices to stabilize key parameters associated with previously learned knowledge while allowing adaptation to new tasks. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance for the combined method. The contribution is both diagnostic and practical: it separates two sources of apparent forgetting and pairs each with a corresponding intervention, instead of treating every decline on an old task as the same kind of failure.
icml-2025-sefe-superficial-and-essential.tldr: SEFE combines answer-style diversification and regularized LoRA updates to address format drift and knowledge loss during continual multimodal instruction tuning.

paragraphs: Fixed image patches can cut across object boundaries and combine unrelated visual content within a token. This paper explores adaptive tokenization at the level of objects and their parts, drawing inspiration from subword tokenization. It examines several segmentation approaches, including superpixels, SAM, and a new tokenizer called EPOC.

EPOC combines boundary detection with watershed segmentation. A compact model handles boundary detection, while the segmentation procedure ensures that every pixel is assigned to a region. Across five datasets, the resulting regions align well with human annotations of objects and parts. The authors report tokens with more coherent semantic content and substantial efficiency advantages.

To test whether these regions improve learning, the researchers design an embedding method for tokens with arbitrary shapes. They train vision-language models with different tokenizers on four datasets covering object recognition and detailed captioning. The results show faster convergence and better generalization with fewer visual tokens. This connects segmentation quality to downstream usefulness: respecting visual boundaries can improve both the representation of an image and the efficiency with which a model learns from it.
icml-2025-subobject-level-image-tokeniza.tldr: EPOC creates image tokens aligned with objects and parts, enabling tested vision-language models to learn faster and generalize better with fewer tokens.

paragraphs: Similarity learning usually measures relationships between individual observed data points. This paper argues that finite training samples leave much of the surrounding sample space uncovered, limiting how well a learned distance generalizes. It proposes representing each example as a data ball with a predictable volume, extending the comparison beyond the observed point itself.

Volume-aware distance measures geometric similarity between these regions. This allows learning to account for relationships among observed examples and their unsampled neighbors. The central idea is to give each training example a surrounding region of influence, so that similarity learning covers more of the sample space without relying only on point-to-point comparisons.

The authors prove that their formulation tightens the error bound of traditional similarity learning and preserves important topological properties. Experiments across multiple data domains report improvements over existing approaches in both supervised and unsupervised tasks. The theoretical and empirical results support region-based similarity as a way to improve generalization, linking the geometry around training examples to performance beyond the exact instances observed during learning.
icml-2025-volume-aware-distance-for-robu.tldr: Volume-aware distance compares regions around data points, improving sample-space coverage and yielding stronger theoretical bounds and empirical similarity-learning results.

paragraphs: Harmful fine-tuning can undermine a language model's safety alignment. This paper finds that the damage is uneven: certain subsets of alignment data are consistently more likely to be forgotten across different fine-tuning tasks. Treating all alignment examples equally therefore overlooks differences in how vulnerable their associated safety behavior is.

Vulnerability-Aware Alignment measures this vulnerability and separates examples into vulnerable and invulnerable groups. It uses group distributionally robust optimization to encourage balanced learning. An adversarial sampler draws examples from whichever group is currently underperforming, while group-dependent adversarial perturbations provide an additional training intervention tailored to the groups.

Experiments across four fine-tuning tasks show significantly reduced harmful scores while preserving downstream task performance, outperforming the state-of-the-art baselines considered. These findings support adapting alignment training to observed vulnerability patterns. The method's distinctive contribution is to make uneven forgetting an explicit training concern: it directs attention toward the weaker group as learning proceeds, rather than assuming that equal treatment of individual examples will produce equally robust safety behavior.
icml-2025-vulnerability-aware-alignment-.tldr: VAA groups alignment examples by vulnerability and targets underperforming groups, reducing harm after fine-tuning while preserving task performance in experiments.
